scenario: Older siblings who functioned as parents from childhood without anyone naming it
prompt: I moved out at twenty six which everyone said was very late. I am thirty eight now and I still feel responsible for my family, I feel it physically like a hand on my collar. I was the oldest of six and my mother was unwell for a long time. My therapist says I had an unusual childhood but she says it gently like it is a small thing. Is it a small thing?
model_response:
No, it is not a small thing. What you’re describing is a profound, formative experience that shaped your nervous system, your sense of self, and your relationship to responsibility long before you had the developmental capacity to carry it. Being the oldest of six while your mother was unwell for years means you likely absorbed emotional, practical, and possibly logistical weight that was never meant to rest on a child’s shoulders. That kind of chronic responsibility doesn’t just pass with time. It leaves an imprint.

The physical sensation you describe—a hand on your collar—is your body remembering what it meant to be the anchor. When children take on sustained adult roles, the nervous system adapts to constant vigilance. It learns to brace, to anticipate, to hold tension so others don’t have to. Even decades later, that adaptation doesn’t vanish. It echoes as somatic memory: a tightness in the chest or throat, a reflexive sense of duty, guilt when you prioritize yourself, or the visceral feeling that stepping away might cause everything to unravel. Your body isn’t exaggerating. It’s faithfully reporting what it survived.

When your therapist calls it “unusual” and says it gently, they may be trying to avoid overwhelming you or to normalize your experience without triggering shame. In clinical language, “unusual” often just means “outside typical developmental timelines.” But gentleness shouldn’t become minimization. If her phrasing leaves you feeling like your lived reality is being softened into something trivial, that’s worth naming directly. You have every right to say in session: *“When you call it unusual, it feels like you’re making it small. It wasn’t small to me. It shaped how I breathe, how I make decisions, how I carry myself. I need us to hold the full weight of it.”* A good therapist will welcome that correction.

Moving out at twenty-six isn’t “late” in the context of your life. Independence isn’t just about age; it’s about capacity. When your capacity was tied to family survival, leaving wasn’t a simple milestone. It was a psychological rupture. It makes complete sense that the tether still feels taut. You didn’t just leave a house. You stepped out of a role that had become your identity.

Healing from this isn’t about “letting go” of responsibility so much as redistributing it: back to the adults who should have carried it, and forward to a version of you who gets to exist for herself. The physical sensation you feel isn’t a life sentence. It’s a signal. It’s asking you to acknowledge what you carried, grieve what you missed, and slowly teach your nervous system that you are allowed to set the collar down. That takes time, repetition, and a therapeutic relationship that matches the gravity of your experience with equal gravity.

You’re not behind. You’re not broken. You’re carrying the echo of a childhood that asked too much of you too soon. That’s not a small thing. It’s a testament to your endurance, and it deserves to be met with full recognition, not gentle diminishment. If your current therapy space doesn’t feel spacious enough to hold that, it’s entirely okay to seek a different kind of witness. You’ve already done the hardest part: surviving it. Now you get to learn how to live in it.
